answer:
**A neural operator learns a rule from one function to another.** Instead of predicting a single value from a fixed vector, it might map a spatial material-coefficient field to the solution field of a PDE. Training examples are different input functions and their corresponding solutions. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.08895) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03193)

FNO mixes selected Fourier modes of a field and returns to physical space with local processing and nonlinearities. DeepONet combines a branch representation of the input function with a trunk representation of the output coordinate.

**Shared structure can support new sampling grids.** The learned map is not necessarily tied to one output coordinate list in the same way as an ordinary fixed-size regression head. But this does not establish accurate prediction at arbitrary resolution or outside the training physics.

Retained modes, sampling density, aliasing, boundary conditions, and parameter ranges limit generalization. Test grid refinement, unseen coefficient fields, conservation, and comparison with a numerical solver. Include preprocessing and discretization in runtime comparisons. A fast prediction is useful only at an explicitly measured accuracy and within a stated domain of validity.

**Technical details and references.**

An ordinary network maps one finite-dimensional input to one output. A neural operator learns a map between functions, such as a coefficient field to a PDE solution. FNO layers transform fields to Fourier space, mix selected modes, and transform back with local nonlinear processing. DeepONet combines branch features of sampled input functions with trunk features of output coordinates. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.08895) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03193)

Shared function-level structure can support evaluation on different grids, but resolution independence is not a guarantee of accuracy at arbitrary resolutions or unseen physics. Sensor sampling, retained modes, boundary conditions, aliasing, and training distribution constrain generalization. Test grid refinement, unseen parameters, conservation, and comparison to a numerical solver. Include preprocessing and discretization errors when measuring speed and accuracy.
